title: The colors of the spirit
hook: nature always wears the colors of the spirit (Nature 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the woods: Emerson says that there we return to reason and faith. Your line was in the woods. Which tree did you stop under? Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

Snow puddles. Twilight. A cloudy sky. A bare, open stretch of town land with nothing on it. Emerson is crossing it, and no special good fortune is on his mind, he says so himself. And yet: "I have enjoyed a perfect exhilaration. I am glad to the brink of fear." On the dullest ground in town, at the dullest hour, he's almost frightened by how happy he is. Same snow, same puddles anyone else would curse. So where did the gladness come from? Today, the colors of the spirit.
screen: `SNOW PUDDLES AT TWILIGHT.` → `NOTHING SPECIAL HAPPENED.` → `GLAD TO THE BRINK OF FEAR.`

segments.voice: First, where the delight lives. Later in the same chapter, Emerson says it plainly: the power to produce this delight does not reside in nature, but in man, or in a harmony of both. The landscape doesn't hand out joy on its own. Something in the one looking has to meet it. Second, the line. "Nature always wears the colors of the spirit." The same field can look like a gift or a wasteland, depending on who's crossing it. Third, he doesn't only mean happy colors. "To a man laboring under calamity, the heat of his own fire hath sadness in it." The fire is the same fire. It's warm. But to someone in trouble, even warmth looks sad. And he goes further: there is a kind of contempt for the landscape, he says, felt by someone who has just lost a dear friend to death. The sky itself seems less grand. These are not the words of a man who's never grieved. Fourth, what to do with this. It's not a scolding, and it's not a trick of positive thinking. It's a description. If the street looks gray today, part of the gray may be yours. That isn't a failure. It's information. And it works the other way: some afternoon the laundromat might look almost holy, and that may be yours too. Knowing that the view wears your colors lets you hold your moods a little more lightly. The field hasn't changed. You have, for now.
screen: `THE DELIGHT ISN'T ONLY IN NATURE.` · `NATURE WEARS THE SPIRIT'S COLORS.` · `EVEN THE FIRE HAS SADNESS IN IT.` · `THE GRAY MAY BE YOURS.` · then, large: `NATURE ALWAYS WEARS THE COLORS OF THE SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how your mood colors the view. Look at whatever is in front of you, a wall, a window, a street. First, just see it. Then ask: what's my mood right now? Tired, easy, tense, hopeful? Look again, and notice how that mood is tinting what you see. Don't try to change the mood. Just see the color it's lending the room. Then let the breath settle and look one more time. The bell holds the time.
The colors of the spirit. Emerson's claim that nature always wears them: the same field, the same fire, looks glad or grieving depending on the one who sees. Today's word.
screen: `THE COLORS OF THE SPIRIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the colors of the spirit. Today, when a place looks dreary or bright, ask how much of that color you brought with you. Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson sometimes use this passage from Nature to notice how mood shapes what they see, checking their own state before deciding a place or a day is dreary.

fork.setup: you're crossing a bare, muddy patch of ground at twilight, with no special good fortune on your mind. what does Emerson say he felt there?

a perfect exhilaration, glad to the brink of fear.
fork.reveal: on the dullest ground at the dullest hour, he was almost frightened by how glad he was. the gladness came from the one crossing.

trapdoor: what you thought: the colors of the spirit is a pretty phrase about sunsets.
what it means: Emerson says the view wears the mood of the one seeing it, glad or grieving.
what a scholar hears: he places the power to delight not in nature alone but in us, or in a harmony of both, and includes grief's colors too.
